chapter: Ch 7: Accounting Standards Based on Items Impacting Financial Statements
unit: Unit 2: AS 5 Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Introduction and Scope of AS 5
explain: AS 5 standardizes how enterprises classify and disclose P&L items for uniform financial reporting.
It enhances comparability of financial statements over time and across different enterprises.
AS 5 does not cover tax implications arising from extraordinary, prior period, or policy adjustments.
All recognized income and expenses in a period must be included in determining net profit or loss.
Net profit or loss comprises ordinary activities, extraordinary items, and prior period adjustments.

flow.title: Components of Net Profit or Loss
steps: Recognize all period income and expenses
Classify into Ordinary Activities
Separate out Extraordinary Items
Include Prior Period Items
Arrive at Net Profit or Loss

topics.example: A firm includes sales revenue, rent expenses, fire damage loss, and past tax error adjustments in its annual P&L.
remember: Tax implications of AS 5 adjustments are handled separately based on applicable tax laws.
mistakes: Excluding regular operational income or expenses from P&L determination.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of AS 5?
o: To prescribe uniform classification and disclosure in profit and loss statements
To establish guidelines for dividend payments
quiz.why: AS 5 prescribes P&L classification and disclosure so enterprises present statements uniformly for comparability.

quiz.q: Which of the following is excluded from the scope of AS 5?
quiz.why: AS 5 explicitly states that it does not deal with tax implications of extraordinary or prior period items.

topics.title: Profit or Loss from Ordinary Activities and Exceptional Items
explain: Ordinary activities are business operations undertaken by an enterprise as part of its regular business.
Profits on merchandise sales or end-of-season inventory write-offs belong to ordinary activities.
Exceptional items are ordinary items whose size, nature, or incidence makes them material to explain performance.
Exceptional items require separate disclosure on the face of P&L or in notes to accounts.
Examples include inventory write-downs to NRV, restructuring provisions, PPE disposals, and litigation settlements.

flow.title: Identifying Exceptional Items
steps: Identify item within ordinary business activities
Evaluate size, nature, or frequency
Assess impact on user understanding of performance
Disclose item separately in financial statements

topics.example: A manufacturing firm writes down damaged inventory by ₹5,00,000; this material ordinary item is disclosed separately.
remember: The term 'Exceptional item' is not defined in AS 5 text but is used for clear disclosure of material ordinary items.
mistakes: Classifying a material ordinary item like an inventory write-down as an extraordinary item.

quiz.q: Which of the following requires separate disclosure as an exceptional item under AS 5?
o: Write-down of inventories to net realizable value
Attachment of property by court order
Correction of mathematical error in past P&L
quiz.why: Write-down of inventory to NRV is an ordinary activity item of such size or nature that separate disclosure is required.

quiz.q: How should an additional GST demand paid for ordinary consultancy services be treated?
o: As an ordinary expense disclosed separately if material
As a change in accounting policy
quiz.why: Tax on ordinary consultancy services is an ordinary activity expense, not an extraordinary item.

topics.title: Extraordinary Items
explain: Extraordinary items are income or expenses arising from events clearly distinct from ordinary business activities.
They are not expected to recur frequently or regularly.
The nature and amount of each extraordinary item must be separately disclosed in P&L or notes.
Classification depends on the nature of the business, not just frequency of occurrence.
Earthquake losses are extraordinary for a factory, but earthquake claims are ordinary for an insurer.
Examples include attachment of company property and losses caused by natural disasters.

flow.title: Test for Extraordinary Classification
steps: Identify event causing gain or loss
Check if event is distinct from main business
Verify if event is non-recurring in nature
Report separately as Extraordinary Item in P&L

topics.example: A severe flood damages a textile factory's machinery; the resulting loss is treated as an extraordinary item.
remember: Whether an event is extraordinary depends on the company's nature of business, not just frequency.
mistakes: Classifying a change in depreciation method as an extraordinary expense.

quiz.q: Which event qualifies as an extraordinary item for a typical manufacturing company?
o: Loss due to attachment of property by court order
quiz.why: Attachment of property by court order is clearly distinct from ordinary business activities.

quiz.q: Claims paid by an insurance enterprise due to an earthquake are classified as:
quiz.why: For an insurance firm insuring such risks, earthquake claims arise from its ordinary business activities.

topics.title: Prior Period Items
explain: Prior period items are current period income or expenses caused by errors or omissions in past financial statements.
Errors arise from mathematical mistakes, wrong policy application, misinterpretation of facts, or oversight.
Infrequent in nature, prior period items are distinct from revisions in accounting estimates.
They must be separately disclosed in P&L to show their exact impact on current profit or loss.
They are normally included in current P&L or shown after determining current net profit or loss.

flow.title: Identifying and Reporting Prior Period Items
steps: Discover past omission or mathematical error
Confirm error relates to previous financial years
Quantify financial impact on current period
Disclose separately in P&L statement

topics.example: A company discovers two inventory sheets worth ₹14.5 lakhs were left out during last year's valuation; it is a prior period item.
remember: Writing off a 5-year-old unpayable creditor balance is a current business decision, not a prior period error.
mistakes: Confusing a revision of estimate based on new information with a prior period error correction.

quiz.q: Prior period items arise due to which of the following reasons?
o: New information about a customer debt
Errors or omissions in preparing past financial statements
Revision of useful life of asset
quiz.why: AS 5 defines prior period items as those arising from errors or omissions in past financial statements.

quiz.q: An audit reveals opening stock was understated by ₹5 lakhs due to a counting error in the previous year. How should this be handled?
o: Treat as a prior period adjustment with separate disclosure
Treat as a change in accounting policy
quiz.why: Counting errors in past inventory valuation are prior period items requiring separate disclosure in current P&L.

topics.title: Changes in Accounting Estimates
explain: Estimates are approximations based on available facts that require revision as new information emerges.
Revisions in estimates do not make adjustments prior period items or extraordinary items.
The effect of a change in estimate is included in net profit/loss in the period of change (and future periods if affected).
Retain original P&L classification (e.g. ordinary or extraordinary) when reporting the estimate change effect.
Material changes in estimates must be disclosed; if quantification is impracticable, state that fact.
If it is difficult to distinguish a policy change from an estimate change, treat it as a change in estimate.

flow.title: Accounting Treatment of Change in Estimate
steps: Obtain new information or experience
Recalculate estimated useful life or provision
Determine current and future period impact
Recognize prospectively in P&L statement

topics.example: Reducing a machine's remaining useful life from 5 years to 2 years due to wear increases depreciation prospectively.
remember: AS 10 (Revised) mandates reviewing useful life and residual value of assets at each year-end as estimate changes.
mistakes: Restating past years' financial statements when an accounting estimate is revised.

quiz.q: A change in the estimated useful life of a depreciable asset affects:
o: Current period only or current and future periods
quiz.why: Revisions of accounting estimates are accounted for prospectively in current and future affected periods.

quiz.q: If it is difficult to distinguish between a change in accounting policy and a change in accounting estimate, how is it treated?
o: As a change in accounting estimate
As a change in accounting policy
quiz.why: AS 5 explicitly mandates treating ambiguous changes as changes in accounting estimates.

topics.title: Changes in Accounting Policies
explain: Accounting policies are specific principles and methods applied in preparing and presenting financial statements.
Policy changes are allowed ONLY if required by statute, for AS compliance, or for more appropriate presentation.
Introducing a formal gratuity scheme replacing ad hoc ex-gratia payments is NOT a policy change.
Adopting a policy for newly occurring or immaterial past events is NOT a policy change.
Material policy changes require disclosure of financial impact; if un-ascertainable, state the fact.
Transition provisions of specific standards govern adoption changes unless standard specifies otherwise.

flow.title: Valid Grounds for Policy Change
steps: Check if change is required by Statute
OR required for Accounting Standard compliance
OR results in better P&L presentation
Apply new policy and disclose material impact

topics.example: Switching inventory valuation from FIFO to Weighted Average to reflect better presentation is a policy change.
remember: Adopting policies for brand-new events or previously immaterial events are not changes in accounting policy.
mistakes: Assuming management can change accounting policies freely without satisfying statutory grounds.

quiz.q: An enterprise can change its accounting policy under AS 5 when:
o: Management wants to alter net profit
Required by statute or for AS compliance
Tax authorities request a temporary shift
quiz.why: AS 5 permits policy changes only if required by statute, AS compliance, or for more appropriate presentation.

quiz.q: Introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments is:
o: Not a change in accounting policy
quiz.why: Adopting an accounting policy for events differing in substance from past events is explicitly not a policy change.
